newsitem.title: UK: UK economic outlook encouraging, BOE's George says.
newsitem.headline: UK economic outlook encouraging, BOE's George says.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Thursday Britain's economic prospects for the next two years were very encouraging but he warned that the country had wasted favourable situations in the past.
In a speech prepared for delivery at Loughborough University, he also said he felt "a good deal more comfortable" with the present monetary policy framework than he had with previous arrangements.

George said the results of the present monetary framework, introduced in 1992, had been encouraging, with underlying inflation averaging 2.7 percent since then, activity growing consistently for 18 successive quarters and unemployment falling almost month by month.
"The prospect for the next two years -- the extent of most forecasting horizons -- remains very encouraging, with most forecasters predicting continuing steady growth with low inflation," he said.

George said that while the present framework had started off at a time when there was some slack in the economy and the world-wide inflationary climate had been helpful, it had not all been plain sailing.

"We have, for example, had to contend with a sharp rise in world commodity prices last year as well as weak economic activity in continental Europe. And, more generally, I would have to say that we have contrived to throw away strong hands before. So time alone will tell."
"But I am very hopeful...and I feel a good deal more comfortable with the monetary framework that we have today than I have at most times in the past."
George outlined in detail the way the present monetary framework works.

It involves an explicit inflation target, quarterly inflation reports by the Bank of England which are not seen by the Treasury before being printed and a monthly meeting between the Governor and the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the minutes of which are published with a six-week time lag.
"This meeting is sometimes represented as a rather casual affair lasting no more than an hour at which we might almost toss a coin. The reality is not quite like that," George said.
"In fact, the monthly meeting comes at the end of a rather lengthy and rigorous process, structured in relation to our receipt of the key monthly economic, monetary and financial data."
The central bank chief's prepared text made no mention of the latest Inflation Report, publised on Wednesday, in which the Bank said interest rates would probably have to rise further in due course.
